info.name: Cocos Trading API
info.description:
A hands-on tour of the Cocos trading API: a portfolio read, instrument search, order submission,
cash transfers and order cancellation, with the happy paths first in each folder and then the
edge cases and errors that are worth seeing.

### Running it

1. Start the stack: `docker compose --profile app up --build`, and wait for the app to be healthy.
2. Check the `baseUrl` variable below (`http://localhost:8080` by default).
3. Run folder **0** to confirm the service answers, then go through the folders in order.

Every request carries a short note on what it is showing and a handful of tests, so the
Collection Runner gives you a pass/fail sweep of the whole API in one go.

### What the figures assume

Folders 0 to 2 are read-only and can be re-run freely. Folders 3 to 5 **write**: their requests
are ordered, and the numbers they assert follow from running them once against the freshly
seeded dataset. To get back to that state:

```
docker compose down -v
docker compose --profile app up --build
```

Without a reset, a second pass will fail on the figures (and on the cancellations, which can
only happen once) - that is the state having moved, not the API misbehaving.

### Conventions worth knowing before you start

* **A rejection is an outcome, not an error.** An order or withdrawal the account cannot cover
  is *stored* with status `REJECTED` and a machine-readable reason, and answered `201`. A request
  that could not be acted on at all writes nothing and comes back `400`, `404` or `409`.
* **`null` means unknown, `0` means zero.** A figure the API cannot know - the price of an
  instrument that does not quote, the return on a negative position - is `null`, never `0`.
* **Errors are `application/problem+json`** with a `title`, `status` and a `detail` that names
  the rule that refused the request.
* **`Idempotency-Key` is optional on every write.** Repeating a request with the same key
  returns the first outcome instead of acting again; reusing a key for a *different* request is
  a `409`. Keys are scoped per user and shared across all three write endpoints.
* **There is no authentication.** The user id in the path is taken at face value, which is why
  the "someone else's order" case below is about user isolation only.

item.name: 0. Service
item.description: A first call to confirm the API is listening before anything else runs.

item.name: The service is up

request.description:
If this fails, nothing below will run. Start the stack with
`docker compose --profile app up --build` and wait for the app container to report healthy.

item.name: 1. Portfolio
item.description:
`GET /api/v1/users/{userId}/portfolio` — what the user owns and what they can spend.

Read-only: these requests can be run in any order, as often as you like, and the figures
asserted here are the ones of the freshly seeded dataset.

item.name: The seeded user

request.description:
The happy path.

`settledCash` is the accounting balance; `availableCash` is what can be spent right now, which
is lower because two pending limit buys are holding pesos. The difference between the two is
exactly what those pending orders commit, so the response reconciles on its own:
`totalAccountValue` = `settledCash` + the sum of every position's `marketValue`.

Positions come in ticker order. Pesos are cash, never a position, so there is no ARS row.

Worth a look at the application log while this runs: the seeded ledger holds a short position
(BMA, -10), and it is reported as a negative quantity rather than hidden.

exec: pm.test("Cash figures of the seeded account", function () {
pm.test("Pending buy orders hold 125500.00 of the settled cash", function () {
pm.test("The response reconciles: settled cash + market values = total", function () {
var sum = p.positions.reduce(function (acc, pos) { return acc + pos.marketValue; }, 0);
pm.test("Three positions, in ticker order", function () {
pm.test("Pesos are cash, not a position", function () {
pm.test("A short position is reported, not hidden", function () {
pm.test("A long position carries its return on the user's own cost", function () {

item.name: The same read again agrees, byte for byte

request.description:
Nothing was traded in between, so the answer must be identical to the previous request —
position order included. A portfolio read that drifts between two calls is a bug.

Run this one right after the request above.

exec: pm.test("Identical to the previous read", function () {

item.name: A user who has never traded

request.description:
An empty account is a valid account: 200, no positions, and zeros.

The zeros are the point. These values are *known* to be zero, so they are reported as `0.00`
rather than as `null`, which the API keeps for figures it genuinely does not know.

item.name: An id that is not a user

request.description:
The edge case that matters next to the request above: a wrong id must not be served as a real
account that happens to be empty. One is a 404, the other a 200 full of zeros.

item.name: A malformed user id

request.description:
`abc` is not an id at all. It is refused at the edge with a 400 and never reaches the domain —
a malformed request is not a missing user.

item.name: 2. Instrument search
item.description:
`GET /api/v1/instruments/search?query=...` - find something to trade.

Read-only, so run these in any order. `query` is required; `page` and `size` are optional.
The response always says which page you got, how big it is and how many instruments matched in
total, so a client knows what it has not seen yet.

item.name: An exact ticker

request.description:
The happy path. One match, and it carries the `instrumentId` that the order endpoint takes, so
you can go from a search straight to an order without a second lookup.

`size` 20 is the deployment's default page size, echoed back so it is visible without a
settings endpoint.

exec: pm.test("Carries a price and the daily move", function () {
pm.test("Page metadata: page 0, default size 20, 1 match", function () {

item.name: A partial ticker, in lower case

request.description:
Matching folds case and looks for the fragment anywhere in the value, not only at the start.
Same instrument as the request above.

exec: pm.test("Finds PAMP from a lower-case fragment", function () {

item.name: Surrounding whitespace is trimmed

request.description:
A query arriving with spaces around it is trimmed before it is searched, and the response echoes
what was actually searched: `pamp`, not `  pamp  `.

exec: pm.test("Searched the trimmed query, and says so", function () {

item.name: A name fragment returns the whole family

request.description:
Search looks at names too, not only tickers. None of these four tickers contains "banco" -
all four match on their name.

exec: pm.test("Matches, in ticker order: BBAR BHIP BMA BPAT", function () {

item.name: An accented name, typed with the accent

request.description:
The accented query finds Molinos Rio de la Plata (spelled with the accent in the dataset).
Compare with the next request.

exec: pm.test("Finds MOLI by its accented name", function () {

item.name: The same name, typed without the accent

request.description:
Accents are **not** folded, so the unaccented query is a different query: MOLI is absent here,
and the matches are three other instruments whose names contain a plain "rio".

A deliberate trade-off rather than an oversight - MOLI stays reachable by its ticker or by
"molinos". Worth knowing if you expected accent-insensitive search.

exec: pm.test("Matches, in ticker order: BHIP OEST RICH", function () {
pm.test("MOLI is not here: accents are not folded", function () {

item.name: Results come in ticker order

request.description:
The order is deterministic - ticker ascending - so paging is stable and two identical requests
never shuffle their results.

exec: pm.test("Matches, in ticker order: AGRO GCLA GGAL GRIM LOMA MOLA OEST PGR SUPV", function () {
pm.test("Sorted, checked independently of the expected list", function () {

item.name: Nothing matched is not an error

request.description:
The search ran and found nothing, which is an answer, not a failure: 200 with an empty list and
a total of 0. Contrast with the rejected queries at the end of this folder, where the search
never ran at all.

exec: pm.test("An empty page, and it says the total is 0", function () {

item.name: A typo matches nothing

request.description:
"bnaco" is "banco" with two letters swapped. Matching is literal: the API does not guess at what
you meant, it tells you nothing matched.

item.name: Cash is never a search result

request.description:
Pesos are the currency instruments are paid in, not something you can buy, so the ARS row is
excluded from search. "pesos" comes back empty for the same reason.

exec: pm.test("ARS is not offered as tradable", function () {

item.name: An instrument with no price is still an instrument

request.description:
PGR has no market data. It is still returned - prices are looked up after the match, so a
missing price can never make an instrument disappear - with `close` and `dailyReturnPercent`
as `null`.

`null`, not `0`: the price is unknown, and that is a different statement from "it is zero".

exec: pm.test("PGR is returned with unknown figures as null", function () {

item.name: A known zero is a different answer from an unknown one

request.description:
The counterpart to PGR. AGRO closed flat, so its daily return is a real, measured `0.00` and its
close is a real number. Neither is `null`, because neither is unknown.

(Two instruments match here - Molinos Agro comes along for the ride.)

exec: pm.test("A measured zero is reported as 0.00", function () {

item.name: A broad query is paged, and says how much there is

request.description:
59 instruments match. You get the first 20 and the total, which is what lets a client decide
whether to keep asking.

exec: pm.test("First page of 59 matches across 3 pages", function () {

item.name: The last page

request.description: 19 results: 20 + 20 + 19 = 59. Nothing repeated from the earlier pages, nothing skipped.

exec: pm.test("The tail of the result set", function () {

item.name: A page past the last one

request.description: An empty page, not a 404. A client that overshoots learns the real total instead of an error.

item.name: A page size above the maximum is clamped, not refused

request.description:
Asking for 500 results gets you the maximum the deployment allows - 100 - and the response says
`size: 100` so you can see what you actually got. A negative `page` is corrected to 0 the same
way. Out-of-range paging is normalised rather than rejected.

exec: pm.test("Clamped to the maximum in force, and echoed", function () {

item.name: A blank query is rejected

request.description:
Two spaces trim to nothing, so there is no query to run. 400 - and note the difference from the
"ZZZZ" request: there the search ran and matched nothing, here it never ran.

exec: pm.test("Says the query must not be blank", function () {

item.name: A missing query parameter is rejected

request.description: `query` is required. Without it there is nothing to search for.

item.name: 3. Order submission
item.description:
`POST /api/v1/users/{userId}/orders` - buy or sell.

**These requests write.** They are ordered, they assume the freshly seeded dataset, and the
figures asserted below follow from running them top to bottom exactly once. To start over:
`docker compose down -v` and bring the stack up again.

The two shapes to keep in mind:

* a `MARKET` order executes at the instrument's latest close and comes back `FILLED`;
* a `LIMIT` order is validated at the price *you* name, comes back `NEW`, and holds what it
  commits - pesos for a buy, shares for a sell - until it is cancelled. Nothing ever fills it:
  there is no matching engine.

And the distinction worth checking first: an order the user cannot afford is a **recorded
outcome**, so it is stored `REJECTED` and answered `201`. A request that cannot be acted on at
all writes nothing and is answered `400`, `404` or `409`.

item.name: A market buy, by share count

request.description:
The happy path: 100 shares at whatever PAMP last closed at.

You get the execution price back, so you know what you paid without a second call.

exec: pm.test("Filled at the latest close", function () {
pm.test("No rejection reason on a filled order", function () {

item.name: The portfolio reflects the fill

request.description:
100 shares at 925.85 is 92,585.00, so available cash goes from 627,500.00 to 534,915.00 and the
PAMP position grows from 40 shares to 140.

Run this straight after the request above, from the seeded state.

exec: pm.test("Cash and holding moved by exactly the order", function () {

item.name: A market buy, by amount in pesos

request.description:
Same instrument, but expressed as "spend up to 100,000.00" instead of a share count.

100,000.00 / 925.85 is 108.008..., so you get **108** shares and 99,991.80 moves. The amount is
a ceiling, not a target: the leftover 8.20 is neither spent nor an error, and no fraction of a
share is ever traded. The derived share count comes back on the order.

exec: pm.test("Derived 108 shares by flooring, not rounding", function () {

item.name: A limit buy holds the cash it commits

request.description:
Validated against your 900.00, never against the market price, and left `NEW`.

It does not spend anything - settled cash does not move - but it reserves 90,000.00, which comes
off `availableCash`. That is what stops two orders from committing the same pesos twice. Compare
the next portfolio read if you want to see it.

exec: pm.test("Resting at the caller's price", function () {

item.name: A limit sell, by amount, at your own price

request.description:
The interesting corner of amount-based sizing: 30,000.00 at the 1,000.00 *you* named derives
**30** shares, not the 32 the same amount would buy at the 925.85 close.

The price in the request substitutes for the market price on both sides of the calculation.

exec: pm.test("Sized at the caller's price: 30 shares, not 32", function () {

item.name: Not enough cash is recorded, not refused

request.description:
1,000 PAMP costs more than the account has available.

The order **is stored**, with the price and the size that were asked for, as `REJECTED` with a
machine-readable reason - and answered `201`, because something was written. No figure in the
portfolio moves.

exec: pm.test("Stored as a rejection, with the reason", function () {

item.name: Selling shares you do not hold is recorded too

request.description:
The same treatment on the other side: a sell larger than the available holding is stored
`REJECTED`, with a reason that says which constraint failed.

exec: pm.test("Rejected for holdings, not for funds", function () {

item.name: A market order for an instrument that does not quote

request.description:
PGR has no market price, so there is no price at which a market order could execute. Refused,
and nothing is written.

This is a judgement call rather than an obvious rule - the alternative would be to invent a
price or to fill at zero - so the error says exactly why.

exec: pm.test("Explains that there is no execution price", function () {

item.name: The same instrument as a limit order is fine

request.description:
The counterpart to the request above. Naming your own price is the honest way to ask for
something the market has not priced, and a limit order never reads market data at all.

item.name: A market order carrying a price

request.description:
A market order executes at the close and takes no price, so a request that sends one is
contradictory. It is refused rather than silently ignored - quietly dropping a field the caller
cared about is how you end up with an order nobody meant to place.

exec: pm.test("Says a MARKET order takes no price", function () {

item.name: A limit order without a price

request.description: There is nothing to validate the order against and nothing to rest it at. 400, nothing written.

item.name: Neither a size nor an amount

request.description:
The quantity is **exactly one of** `size` (shares) or `amount` (pesos). With neither, there is
no order to place.

item.name: Both a size and an amount

request.description:
The other half of "exactly one of": two quantities that could disagree are refused rather than
one of them being picked for you.

item.name: Cash is not a tradable instrument

request.description:
Instrument 66 is ARS - the pesos themselves. You cannot buy pesos with pesos, which is also why
it never shows up in search or as a portfolio position. Deposits and withdrawals have their own
endpoint, in the next folder.

item.name: An unknown instrument

request.description: Nothing to trade. 400, nothing written.

item.name: An unknown user

request.description:
The target of the request is a user's order collection, and that user does not exist. 404, not
400: the body was fine, the address was not.

item.name: Idempotency - the first request with a key

request.description:
Send `Idempotency-Key` and the outcome is stored against that key. This is a normal order; the
next two requests are what make it interesting.

The order id is saved into a collection variable so the replay below can compare.

exec: pm.test("A real order was placed", function () {

item.name: The same request again, same key - a retry, not a second order

request.description:
The same order, re-sent with the key after an imaginary timeout. The body here is deliberately
reformatted - different whitespace, different field order, `5.00` instead of `5` - because the
key is matched against the *parsed* request, not against the raw bytes.

You get the first order back: same id, same status, same timestamp. Only one order exists, and
the cash moved once. Check the portfolio if you want to confirm it.

exec: pm.test("Replays the first order rather than placing a new one", function () {

item.name: The same key with a different body - a conflict

request.description:
Size 7 this time, under a key that already stands for the size-5 order. That is a client bug,
and answering either outcome would be wrong, so it is a 409 and nothing is written.

The earlier order is not disclosed in the error.

exec: pm.test("Names the key that was reused", function () {

item.name: The same key, another user - an independent request

request.description:
Keys are scoped per user, so user 2 reusing the same string is not a conflict: the request is
processed on its own merits. User 2 has no cash yet, so it is a recorded rejection.

exec: pm.test("Judged on its own merits, not replayed", function () {

item.name: 4. Cash transfers
item.description:
`POST /api/v1/users/{userId}/cash-transfers` - put pesos in, take pesos out.

**These requests write**, they are ordered, and they all act on **user 2**, who starts with an
empty account in the seeded dataset. Run them top to bottom once.

`side` is `CASH_IN` or `CASH_OUT` and `amount` is a whole number of pesos. The body is closed:
anything else in it is refused. Like orders, a withdrawal the account cannot cover is a recorded
`REJECTED` outcome answered `201`, while a request that cannot be acted on writes nothing.

item.name: A deposit

request.description: The happy path. 100,000.00 in, filled immediately.

item.name: The cash is there

request.description: Both figures are now 100,000.00: the deposit is settled, and nothing is holding any of it.

exec: pm.test("Settled and available cash both 100000.00", function () {

item.name: A withdrawal of one peso more than there is

request.description:
The boundary case. One peso over, so it is stored `REJECTED` with a reason and answered `201`;
the cash does not move.

exec: pm.test("Recorded as rejected, with the reason", function () {

item.name: A withdrawal of exactly what there is

request.description: The other side of the same boundary: emptying the account is allowed.

item.name: Back to an empty account

request.description: Zero again - and zero as a known figure, not as a `null`.

item.name: Idempotency - the first keyed deposit

request.description:
Same mechanism as on orders, and the same key namespace: a key already used for one of this
user's orders would conflict here too.

item.name: The same deposit again - a retry, not a second deposit

request.description:
`100000.00` is the same amount as `100000`, so this is the same request: you get the first
transfer back instead of depositing twice.

item.name: And the money arrived once

request.description: 100,000.00, not 200,000.00. This is the assertion that actually proves the retry was safe.

item.name: The same key for a different transfer - a conflict

request.description: A withdrawal under the key that stands for a deposit. 409, nothing written.

item.name: An amount with centavos

request.description:
Transfers are whole pesos. 100.50 is refused rather than rounded - rounding someone's money
without telling them is not an option.

exec: pm.test("Says it must be whole pesos", function () {

item.name: An order's side on this endpoint

request.description:
`BUY` is a perfectly good side - for an order. Here it means nothing, and the error says what
the alternatives are.

exec: pm.test("Lists the sides that do apply", function () {

item.name: A field that belongs to an order

request.description:
A transfer carries only `side` and `amount`. An `instrumentId` here means the caller thinks they
are placing an order, so it is refused and nothing is written.

Note the asymmetry with order submission, which ignores fields it does not know: the stricter
rule is on the endpoint that moves money in and out of the system.

item.name: 5. Order cancellation
item.description:
`POST /api/v1/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}/cancel` - take a pending order back. No body.

**These requests write**, they are ordered, and they act on the two limit buys that user 1 has
resting in the seeded dataset: order 5 (LOMA) and order 7.

Only a `NEW` order can be cancelled. A cancellation releases what the order was holding, so it
shows up as available cash again on the next portfolio read, while settled cash does not move -
nothing was ever spent.

item.name: What is held before cancelling

request.description:
A baseline, saved into a collection variable, so the next requests can show the exact effect of
a cancellation without depending on what you ran earlier.

exec: pm.test("Some cash is held by pending orders", function () {

item.name: Cancel a pending buy

request.description:
The happy path. Order 5 is a limit buy of 50 LOMA at 710.00, resting `NEW`; it comes back
`CANCELLED`, with no rejection reason - it was not rejected, it was withdrawn.

item.name: The cash it was holding is free again

request.description:
50 shares at 710.00 is 35,500.00, and that is exactly how much more is available now. Settled
cash is untouched, because a pending order never spent anything.

exec: pm.test("Available cash grew by exactly 35500.00", function () {
pm.test("Settled cash did not move", function () {

item.name: Cancelling it again

request.description:
Order 5 is no longer `NEW`, so there is nothing to cancel. 409, and the message says what state
it is actually in.

Note this is *not* what a retry looks like - see the keyed requests below.

exec: pm.test("Says the order is already cancelled", function () {

item.name: Cancelling an order that already filled

request.description: Order 2 executed. The trade happened; it cannot be called back.

exec: pm.test("Says the order is filled", function () {

item.name: Cancelling someone else's order

request.description:
Order 7 exists, but it belongs to user 1, and this request is addressed to user 2's orders.

The answer is a 404 with the *same* message as an order that was never created - a caller cannot
use this endpoint to find out which order ids belong to somebody else. Order 7 stays `NEW`, as
the next request shows.

exec: pm.test("Indistinguishable from a missing order", function () {

item.name: Cancelling an order that does not exist

request.description: Same shape of answer as the request above. That is the point.

item.name: Idempotency - a keyed cancellation

request.description: Order 7 is user 1's other pending buy, cancelled under a key this time.

item.name: The same cancellation again - a retry, not a 409

request.description:
Compare with "cancelling it again" above, which got a 409. The difference is the key: with it,
this is recognisably the same request as the one that already succeeded, so it replays that
answer instead of complaining about the order's state. One cancellation happened, not two.

exec: pm.test("Replays the same cancelled order", function () {

item.name: The same key for a different order - a conflict

request.description:
The key stands for cancelling order 7; this asks it to cancel order 5. 409, and the message
names the key rather than the order's state - the request never got far enough to look at it.

exec: pm.test("Names the key that was reused", function () {
